newsitem.title: FRANCE: French employers' head warns government on wages.
newsitem.headline: French employers' head warns government on wages.

text.p: Jean Gandois, the chairman of the national employers' federation CNPF, warned the new Socialist government against plans to boost economic growth and consumption through wage increases, saying that this would only widen public deficits.
"Boosting consumption through salaries has totally risky consequences. Amid the current climate of pessimism, people will decide to save instead of consuming," he said RTL radio.

"Today it is very difficult to boost growth through consumption without derailing public spending...We cannot boost (consumption) through wages without (sparking) perverse effects that will immediately increase public deficits," he added.
Critics have said the government plans meant higher spending and would jepardize France's chances of meeting the criteria for economic and monetary union.

Jospin has ordered an audit of public finances to see how far France is from cutting its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, a target for countries wanting to join the euro single currency planned in 1999. France's deficit was was 4.2 percent of GDP in 1996.
Gandois also said that a government proposal to reduce working time without loss of pay would be a "serious mistake" as it would hurt the competitiveness of French companies.

"Reducing working hours without loss of pay increases the cost of the working hour and therefore in a country where labour costs are the highest in the world...it curbs the competitiveness of companies, that is the possibility for our country to create wealth and jobs," he said.
Gandois said he was favourable to a "company by company" approach but stressed that "there is no solution if there is not a salary freeze or a cut in wages."

In his maiden speech to parliament, Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin promised to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay over five years and create 700,000 youth jobs, with half in the private sector.
